intro: Mimì and Rodolfo’s introductions become a duet, then a decision to leave together. Nellie Melba and Enrico Caruso recorded this side in 1907; the restoration is by Adam Cuerden, via commons.wikimedia.org, with attribution required.
question: How do two separate introductions become a shared declaration?

cues.title: Two voices, two perspectives
cues.text: Throughout the duet, distinguish Caruso’s tenor from Melba’s soprano, then notice when separate phrases become a shared sonority. The dramatic exchange moves between Rodolfo’s declaration, Mimì’s response and their practical negotiation about going out together.
cues.evidence: DAHR documents soprano–tenor duet with orchestra; the primary Act I libretto supplies the exchange: https://it.wikisource.org/wiki/La_boh%C3%A8me/Quadro_primo . No voice entrance or overlap is placed at a specific second.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The first broad crest
cues.text: The opening expansion reaches a crest and then recedes. Compare the singers’ sustained line with the accompaniment’s movement beneath it; the duet does not need to remain at this early intensity to keep the encounter moving.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/puccini-o-soave-fanciulla.txt: relative level rises from −27.0 dB at 0:00 to −9.8 at 0:35, then falls to −22.8 at 0:50. The trace measures the combined recording, not either singer separately.

cues.title: An attic before the café
cues.text: The lovers meet in a Paris attic on Christmas Eve. Rodolfo’s friends are waiting for him; Mimì asks to accompany them to the Café Momus. The duet therefore leads out of private conversation into the crowded public world of Act II.
cues.evidence: Royal Opera House 2017 programme, Act I synopsis: http://static.roh.org.uk/showings/la-boheme-live-2017/en.pdf . The primary libretto ends with the lovers leaving together; no stage action is timed to this disc.

cues.title: Listen between the declarations
cues.text: Across the middle of the duet, compare sustained song with the shorter exchanges that carry the conversation. The characters still have decisions to make: following the scale of each phrase helps distinguish declaration from reply without treating every line as a separate aria.
cues.evidence: The Act I libretto alternates the longer declarations with short dialogue about joining the friends: https://it.wikisource.org/wiki/La_boh%C3%A8me/Quadro_primo . This is a middle-passage invitation, not a word-aligned identification at 1:45.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Illica and Giacosa’s collaboration
cues.text: Puccini chose Henry Murger’s Parisian stories for La bohème; Luigi Illica and Giuseppe Giacosa shaped the libretto. The opera premiered in Turin on 1 February 1896, eleven years before this New York recording.
cues.evidence: Work, authors and premiere: https://www.puccinifestival.it/en/giacomo-puccini/ . Session: https://adp.library.ucsb.edu/index.php/matrix/refer/200006039 . The year comparison does not imply that these singers participated in the premiere.

cues.title: A later crest, then release
cues.text: The closing span makes another substantial rise before the sound falls away. Compare this later crest with the opening one: the duet’s ending is not simply the first declaration repeated at a lower level.
cues.evidence: The report shows renewed relative-level rises at 2:50–3:00, with its highest five-second window at 3:00, then a fall through 3:10–3:15. No particular final pitch, word or onstage/offstage placement is inferred from the trace.

transitions.title: A broad declaration leaves space for replies
transitions.how: The duet’s text moves from declarations towards short replies and the question of going out. In this listening map, the middle window follows the early expansion and its retreat. Compare the lengths of the vocal phrases and the space the accompaniment occupies between them. The timing is not a verified location of the first conversational line, and no modern orchestral part is assigned to the acoustic session.
transitions.evidence: The report places a strong novelty boundary at 1:28, with changing attack density around it. The primary libretto documents declarations followed by dialogue: https://it.wikisource.org/wiki/La_boh%C3%A8me/Quadro_primo . Its first word is not aligned to 88 seconds.

transitions.title: Separate replies point towards a shared close
transitions.how: The closing listening span passes through a lower-level interval before another broad rise. Keep the dramatic destination in mind: the text ends with the two lovers leaving together and singing their declaration outside. The record’s acoustic balance cannot establish theatrical distance; the useful comparison is between separate replies and the shared ending, not an invented movement of singers away from a microphone.
transitions.evidence: A novelty boundary at 2:38 is followed by a −22.6 dB window at 2:40 and the rise through 2:50–3:00. The libretto supplies the departure, not its precise timing on this side: https://it.wikisource.org/wiki/La_boh%C3%A8me/Quadro_primo .

facts: Lucca; Milan Conservatory, 1880–83, with Antonio Bazzini and Amilcare Ponchielli
Publisher Giulio Ricordi · librettists Luigi Illica and Giuseppe Giacosa · later Giuseppe Adami and Renato Simoni
Twelve operas when the three parts of Il trittico are counted separately; songs, sacred and chamber music
composer.background:
Puccini was born into a dynasty of church musicians in Lucca in 1858. His father Michele died when Giacomo was five, and the expectation that the boy would inherit the family profession survived him. Puccini studied locally, played the organ and composed sacred music, including a Mass completed in 1880. Hearing Verdi’s Aida in Pisa in 1876 helped turn his attention towards the theatre. A scholarship enabled him to enter the Milan Conservatory in 1880, where he studied with Antonio Bazzini and Amilcare Ponchielli. His graduation work, the orchestral Capriccio sinfonico, already contains material he would reuse at the beginning of La bohème.

His first opera, Le Villi, failed to win the Sonzogno competition for which it was written, but a performance in Milan in 1884 attracted the publisher Giulio Ricordi. Ricordi supported revisions, further performances and the much less successful Edgar, premiered at La Scala in 1889. The partnership mattered because Puccini composed slowly, demanded repeated alterations to his texts and needed protection against a premature commercial verdict. The theatre was a collective workshop: librettist, publisher, designer and conductor all contributed practical decisions, although Puccini insisted on controlling the length and placement of the decisive moments.
composer.epithet: An opera composer who made a remembered tune, a stage noise or a change of orchestral register determine the timing of a scene.
